newsitem.title: USA: U.S. financial reform bill needs changing - Ludwig.
newsitem.headline: U.S. financial reform bill needs changing - Ludwig.

text.p: U.S. Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig said on Tuesday that financial reform legislation before Congress "has areas that we think need changing."

The House Banking Committee approved the massive financial reform bill last month by a narrow 28-26 vote and it is now being considered by the House Commerce Committee. The complex proposal would tear down decades-old laws separating banking from insurance and securities underwriting.
Ludwig, responsible for supervising commercial banks, told Reuters during a visit to San Francisco that the bill "has areas that we think need changing."
One such area was "the fact that operating subsidiaries cannot engage in the same kind of activities as holding company affiliates," Ludwig said.
He also singled out the bill's insurance provisions. "Decisions on what's an insurance product, what's a banking product, how that process works, is also something we criticize," he said.
Asked if he would oppose the bill in its current form, he said: "We have not taken a definitive view of the bill as a whole or of every single provision."

Ludwig, in San Francisco to speak at a meeting sponsored by the Directors' Roundtable, is due to testify on the financial reform bill before a congressional subcommittee in Washington later this week.

Ludwig said the U.S. banking system was "as profitable and as well capitalized as we've seen in decades. We regulators are paid worriers so I'm always concerned that we maintain credit quality. We have to watch that very closely and we continue to do that."
James Roethe, executive vice-president and general counsel of BankAmerica Corp, told the meeting that the bank opposed the financial reform bill in its current form.

"If it were to go to the floor today as it came out of the House Banking Committee, we would oppose the bill although we continue to explore approaches to try to make improvements," Roethe said, adding that the bill had good and bad features.
He criticized part of the bill dealing with insurance.

"Banks as opposed to bank holding companies would generally be prohibited from underwriting insurance, insurance products," Roethe said. Also, the definition of insurance "would be left in the hands of state insurance regulators who could challenge the banks' ability to offer products that these regulators assert to be insurance. This we consider to be a step backwards," he said.
The bank was also concerned about the new National Council of Financial Services that would be a part of the bill, Roethe said.

In his speech to the roundtable, Ludwig posed the question of whether, in light of fundamental changes in the financial services marketplace, the principles underlying the Community Reinvestment Act should be extended to cover the broader financial services industry. He said he hoped for a public discussion on this issue.
